real: The U.S. and Britain nearly go to war over a single shot pig
source: 1859 — the Pig War: a U.S. settler shot a British-owned pig on disputed territory between the U.S. and Britain, and both nations mobilized troops, bringing the two countries to the brink of war over a pot of pork.

real: In the final days of WWII, German and American soldiers fight together against the Nazis
source: 1945 — the Battle of Castle Itter: in a bizarre last week of the war, Wehrmacht and Waffen-SS soldiers joined forces with U.S. troops to defend a castle holding rescued French war ministers, defeating the Waffen-SS in what is one of the few times the two sides fought as allies.
fakes: Allied and German soldiers briefly become allies in the war's final days

real: A volcano's ash causes a year with no summer — and changes world history
source: 1816 — the 'Year Without a Summer': the 1815 eruption of Mount Tambora cooled the planet so much that New England saw frost in June, harvests failed worldwide, and the misery is often cited as a factor behind Mary Shelley writing Frankenstein.
fakes: A volcanic eruption turns a summer into a winter across a continent

real: A 46-foot stone giant is discovered under a hill in Wales — until it's not
source: The Cardiff Giant — a 46-foot (14 m) stone 'giant' was unveiled as a 'recent discovery' under a hill in Cardiff in 1869 and drew thousands of curious visitors, until the sculptor admitted he'd carved and buried it himself as a publicity stunt.

real: A French soldier eats so much, constantly, that doctors study him
source: Tarrare — an 18th-century French soldier reportedly ate 12 pounds (5 kg) of food a day, along with stones, insects, and live animals, and was eventually 'used' by the military as a living courier who could hide messages in his stomach, becoming a subject of medical fascination.

real: A knot of dead rats found in a sewer turns out to be a real biological thing
source: The 'rat king' — a phenomenon in which several dead rats become tangled together by their fur into a single knot, found in sewers and attics, is a real (if gruesome) occurrence documented since the 1890s, with specimens in museums and an annual 'rat king of the year' contest in some quarters.
